title: The American town inside a rain forest, with whales, gold mining and its own glacier | CNN
summary: No other US capital captures the spirit of adventure quite like Juneau.
author: David Allan
article:
There are no roads leading to Alaska’s capital, leaving just three ways to reach this northwestern Brigadoon by boat, plane or being born here. And you may wish you were born in Juneau because this is, by far, the most visually striking state capital in the US.
Located along the Inside Passage, Juneau is too beautiful, its culture and history too rich, to get cynical about its popularity with the cruisers. By land mass, it is the largest state capital in the nation, its tall peaks remain snow-capped well into summer, seaplanes buzz overhead, local residents include bears, mountain goats and whales. With its remote location and a terrain that’s worlds away from a typical American town experience, it feels like you need a passport. What you need, though, is an insulated rain jacket.
The whole region surrounding Juneau is located inside the incredibly biodiverse Tongass National Forest , the world’s largest intact temperate rainforest. Juneau has around 230 rainy days a year, with June being the sunniest with about 50% wet days.
“It does rain a lot here,” admits Nathan Hickok, a local heavy equipment operator who’s lived in Juneau his whole life, “but one sunny day makes all the wet and cold days totally worth it.”
Juneau is off the beaten track, to say the least. But fortune favors the bold who make it this far. With average summer temperature that peaks in the low 60s, this town on the edge of real wilderness draws in those who love communing with nature and wildlife, unique American history and seafood.
Mendenhall Glacier , which looks like a light blue frozen tsunami rolling through the valley, is remarkably accessible. You can easily see it from the main road north of town, aptly named Glacier Highway. You can hike close to it, dogsled on it, glide into its lake on a boat, kayak or raft, or take a helicopter tour that lands on it.
Like so much of Juneau, it can get crowded in summer and is more peaceful in the spring and fall (and inhospitable in the winter). But the sooner you have this experience the better as it’s quickly receding due to the climate crisis. In fact, as of just last year, it no longer touches the lake it feeds into.
Of Juneau’s more than 1.5 million annual visitors, more than 90% take their first epic glimpse of this town from the deck of a massive cruise ship. Tides of summer cruise ship passengers wash up on its shores, leaving souvenir shops and fleets of excursion busses in their wake. But this year, for the first time, the city is capping the number of people who can disembark to 16,000 on most days, about half the size of Juneau’s population, from a peak estimate of 21,000 souls.
STREAMING NOW: Explore Alaska and its buried treasure
Less accessible and crowded as Mendenhall Glacier but just as dramatic, is the Tracy Arm Fjord, with ice cliffs, waterfalls and the Dawes Glacier. Any boat tour going through it, mainly run by True Alaskan Tours , takes the better part of a day and requires advance booking.
The other big local attraction is the humpback whales growing to about the size of a city bus. In Juneau they graze on krill and other fish in the waters off of Auke Bay after breeding in Hawaii in the winter, a 6,000-mile roundtrip swim. Long summer days – more than 18 hours in June – mean long feeding hours too.
While busloads of cruisers were being herded like sheep around Statter Harbor during a visit in June, the very reasonably priced and family-owned Juneau Whale Tours made a stealthy extraction of its small group of about a dozen passengers (including this writer), quickly pushing off while bigger groups were still in the parking lot, calling roll. Their custom 50-foot-long catamaran features a wraparound deck for paparazzi action.
On this two-hour excursion in early June, whale-watchers lucked out with dry weather and “muggings” (as close encounters of the whale-ish kind are called) by a humpback and pack of orcas.
The orca pack of 10, which surfaced in impressive synchronization, represents such a rare sighting that Captain T.J. Miller asked the passengers not to mention them on social media lest they create an expectation by other groups.
Humpbacks, spotted by 20-foot-high spouts, are the guaranteed stars of the show, breaching and diving in massive tail-waving fashion.
Juneau’s attractions get undeniably busy in high season, but according to Hickok, local nature trails provide a great way to avoid the crowds. “The Alaskan experiences here are endless. There are enough trails here that my wife and I couldn’t get to all of them in the summer if we tried.”
Just as accessible, yet far less visited than Mendenhall Glacier, is Gold Creek Flume Trail. “Hike the flume,” as locals suggest, referring to this easy walking escape above the downtown streets. A boardwalk runs along the spot where a water wheel and generator gave the town its first electric power plant in 1893.
It’s now an Instagram-worthy boardwalk that leads to a waterfall before looping back to town. It’s not unheard of to see a black bear or mountain goat up there as well. With some of the boardwalk being restored, a temporary detour leads into a small trail through fiddlehead ferns and tall, moss-draped spruce and other evergreens, snaking alongside the rapids of Gold Creek. You may get slightly more than you bargained for in the detour, but you’ll emerge from the adventure unscathed if a little muddy . The city hopes to reopen the full trail by August.
Walking back into town , you might easily pass the white, columned governor’s mansion, located on an ordinary residential street. It may remind you of a famous “Saturday Night Live” portrayal of a certain former Alaska governor and the comically false detail that she could “see Russia from my house!”
A little farther out of town, the historic national Perseverance Trail crosses bridges, skirts old mine ruins, and offers stunning rainforest canyon views.
In the north part of town, the Mendenhall Basin Trail runs along the back of the airport (including a water landing strip for floatplanes), and along the beautiful valley, punctuated with far off mountains. On one Sunday morning in June there were only a handful of other visitors enjoying the space until a pack of about a dozen showed up, everyone with cameras. What appeared to be a cruise ship excursion was actually the Juneau chapter of the Audubon Society. This trail skirts the Mendenhall Wetlands Refuge, a prime birding location with 250 species of migratory and resident birds, including large numbers of sandpipers and Canada geese  .
One popular attraction has been closed since April, following an accident that injured two employees. When in operation, the Goldbelt Tramway makes a near vertical leap of 1,800 feet from the cruise ship dock up Mount Roberts. There’s no reopen date yet. You can still climb Roberts, though, via a vigorous 4.5-mile trail.
There’s gold in them thar hills as well. In fact, Juneau, named after Canadian prospector Joe Juneau, probably wouldn’t exist as a town without the gold rush that began in 1880. That’s when Chief Cowee of the Auk Tlingits led prospectors Juneau and Richard Harris to a stream teeming with gold.
In the decades that followed, the town ( briefly called Harrisburgh ) became home to some of the largest gold mining operations in the world.
Channeling “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom,”    you don a hard hat for the first part of the tour inside the ol’ AJ Mine and Gastineau Mill . Although the tour traverses a tiny fraction of the 160 miles of mining tunnel in the local mountains, you’re in there long enough to appreciate the cold, damp, loud and dangerous conditions of the industry in its prime.
One of the guides, Brad — who was born in the Alaska Territory, a year before statehood was approved by Congress in 1959 — reminds visitors that mining isn’t dead, either. While extracting the gold that still lies in AJ Mine has become unprofitable, other nearby mines continue to drill for precious metals. Mining provides well-paying careers that are safer (remote mining from a computer terminal is now a thing) than when they placed sticks of dynamite in the walls by candlelight.
Outside the mine, the tour becomes less engaging. Extraction methods are detailed, followed by panning for your own flecks of the gold stuff, the latter perhaps fun for kids. For more of the fascinating history, head to the compact Juneau-Douglas City Museum in town.
It’s easy to find the mustard yellow building in compact, walkable Juneau. Out front flies a 49-star American flag. Inside, the tour begins with a high-quality 25-minute documentary and primer on the exhibits that follow, which include old mining gear and a plane’s-eye-view of the valley as a 3-D topographical map. You learn that the sale of Alaska from Russia to the US in 1867 meant little to the local Tlingit community whose own land rights went ignored, and that due to the gold rush, Juneau had electricity and telephones before most of the United States.
Next to the museum is the State Capitol building, and in front of it stands a statue of William Henry Seward. It was erected in 2017, on the 150th anniversary of the purchase of Alaska from Russia, derided by some as “Seward’s Folly.” But the discovery of the first significant gold strike – here in Juneau, only 13 years after the sale – gave Secretary of State Seward, who negotiated the deal, the last laugh.
A few blocks from the Juneau museum is the Alaska Museum , with large displays illuminating the lives of the original peoples, decoding ceremonies, clothing and masks. Curious pop culture artifacts include a once-popular gold prospecting boardgame that starts in Seattle and ends in San Francisco, with Alaska in between. Visitors also learn that the Pacific Princess cruise ship toured the Inside Passage before reaching stardom as the real cruise ship seen on the hit 1970s TV show “The Love Boat.”
The Red Dog Saloon is something of a museum piece as well, flirting as it does at the edge of nostalgia and kitsch. Lines sometime form out the swinging saloon doors for the privilege of eatin’ ‘n’ drinkin’ on sawdust-covered floors under taxidermy and wagon wheel lights.
Gunslinger Wyatt Earp’s gun, which legend says was left behind from his visit in 1900, is displayed above the bar. A suspenders-wearing piano player cranks out George M. Cohan tunes while cruise ship patrons throw back the signature shot: the Duck Fart, a sweet concoction of Bailey’s, Kahlúa and Crown Royal. There are three rules to drinking a Duck Fart, says a server in a red, old West dress: no sippin’, no sharin’ and no stirrin’, just “quack, quack and knock that shit back.” It’s hokey but jovial. Unsurprisingly, you exit the saloon through the gift shop.
You may also want to brave the perpetual line at Jellyfish Donuts (247 S. Franklin St.) for the freshest version of the pastry you’ve ever had. They are individually made-to-order so every donut is warm and gooey, a tiny, edible pillow collapsing in on its own hole. Options range from traditional to the inventive, such as the Alaskan Spruce with real, perhaps edible, spruce needles with green, maple-tasting glaze, and a savory salmon donut.
Another popular spot is Deckhand Dave’s Fish Tacos , open seasonally in a festive outdoor food truck space that’s covered from the rain and warmed by firepits. Across the street from Dave’s, the Devil’s Club Brewing Co. is the anti-Red Dog Saloon. You don’t have to be a member of the “club” to enjoy its craft selection of IPA and sandwiches in a modern, chill, uncrowded space.
Tracy’s King Crab Shack , with two popular informal locations — and no longer the actual shack it was less than 20 years ago — is where the masses line up for the impossibly long Alaskan king crab legs, served with warm butter and doughy rolls.
But Captain Miller from the whale tour recommended The Hangar on the Wharf , which serves the same crab legs on its full menu, with fewer crowds and stunning views from its windows. Behind the bar is an IMAX-film scene of otherworldly proportions: A massive stern of a cruise ship next to the snow-peaked mountains across the Gastineau Channel, under big sky.
A series of hand drawn postcards illustrating local activities are sold inside the charming Rainy Retreat Books (13 Seward St.), including one depicting the traditional Russian dumplings and Sriracha sauce of Pel’Meni (2 Marine Way). The tiny spot is located down by the water, across from a pair of tall totem poles. Those waiting patiently for the only thing they sell — warming bowls of beef or potato dumplings — were a more local crowd than inside the neighboring fish and chip shop. When served with “everything,” the dish includes curry powder, sour cream, hot sauce and a slice of marble bread.
Up by the airport, it seems relatively few outsiders have discovered the warm and welcoming Donna’s Restaurant . Old photos of Juneau streets are framed on the walls, ignored by diners in green booths focused on hearty breakfasts of omelets, pancakes, reindeer sausage and bottomless cups of coffee.
There’s no shortage of shops downtown, selling proof you’ve made it this far in your travels, including art galleries and jewelry stores. If a tattoo is more your kind of souvenir, they have a couple of those as well.
Since most visitors are cruise passengers and arrive in Juneau in the room where they’ll sleep, the hotel options for land lubbers are limited. Downtown, the Four Points by Sheraton has great views and the Alaskan Hotel & Bar recreates that pioneer vibe. On the north end of town, Grandma’s Feather Bed , a Best Western property (and a John Denver song), is as cute and comfortable as it sounds. The Victorian-style inn offers well-appointed suites, with full breakfast included. You can even walk to the airport from there, but the free shuttle will take you.
The main road that connects downtown and the airport neighborhood is Egan Drive. Rental cars are pricey but between hotel vans and Ubers you can get around without one. The city bus (#3 and #4), as big as an adult humpback whale, if you recall, runs the 9 miles between the north and south parts. The #8 bus stops 1.5 miles away from the Mendenhall Glacier Visitor Center. It only costs $2 one-way, and takes about 15 minutes more than a car. You may notice a PSA inside the busses reminding residents not to leave garbage outside, in order to keep their bear neighbors wild.
A couple of those bears are taxidermied inside the wee Juneau International Airport, with its five gates and seaplane base. Its commercial options, primarily on Alaska Airlines, include Anchorage and Seattle, about 90 minutes and two hours away, respectively. And you won’t find, anywhere, a friendlier, more good-natured TSA staff than those at JNU.
It’s a small consolation for leaving such a stunning, inspiring and welcoming town.

title: She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World | CNN
summary: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, in modern-day Turkey, was an ornate memorial built for Carian ruler Mausolus and overseen by his sister-wife Artemesia II.
author: Maureen O'Hare
article:

The mountainous Bodrum Peninsula rises over the vibrant blue Aegean Sea, its peak richly forested, its foothills stacked with white flat-roofed homes and hotels.
On the peninsula’s exclusive northern coastline, superyachts bob between the ultra-luxury villas and hotels of Paradise Bay . In Bodrum town on the southern shore, traditional gulet sailing boats fill the marina, ready to take tourists on cruises.
Today, it’s where Istanbul’s elite come to relax, party, or be pampered, and where international visitors travel for sunshine and sea.
They are by no means the first people of means to have left their mark here. From the Leleges to the Mycenaeans, from the Romans to the Byzantines, many civilizations have risen and fallen on the peninsula, leaving archaeological treasures in their wake.
The greatest of all, built around 350 BCE on a hilltop overlooking what is now Bodrum town, was the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It was all the more remarkable because it was created as the result of an incestuous marriage.
Very little remains of the mausoleum today. Today, the biggest historical structure is Bodrum Castle, a huge Gothic fortress overlooking the marina. The region’s importance as a tourism hub is just the latest chapter in its long history of strategic significance.
“It’s like a gateway between East and West,” says Orhan Can, a guide with Bodrum Tour , pointing out that even today Istanbul is the best connected airport in the world. Turkey “has always been a place for business.”
The Mausoleum’s occupants, more than two millennia ago, were Mausolus and his sister-wife Artemesia II, members of the Hectamnod dynasty which ruled over the region then known as Caria between 395 and 366 BCE.
Mausolus and Artemisia made Halicarnassus — now Bodrum — the capital of Caria, boosting its population and initiating many building projects, the most extravagant being their tomb. After Mausolus’s death in 353 BCE, Artemisia oversaw its construction, a temple-like structure designed by the finest Greek architects and sculptors, combining Greek, Egyptian, and Lycian styles.
Decorated with friezes of battle scenes and some 400 freestanding sculptures, its base was more than 400 feet in circumference. It was topped by a pyramid upon which rode a four-horse chariot containing statues of the departed couple.
Artemisia held a grand funeral for her husband, with games and ceremonies. “After Mausolus died, they cremated him,” says Can. Legend has it that Artemesia, the grieving sister-widow, drank her husband’s ashes mixed with wine, which would later become a popular subject for Renaissance painters in the Western world.
She succeeded him as leader, becoming a noted naval commander, but outlived him by just two years. Legend has it that her early death was “because she was so sad,” says Can.
A series of earthquakes from the 12th to 15th century led to the monument’s collapse. At Bodrum Mausoleum Museum , visitors to the archaeological park look down, not up, into the sunken foundations excavated by British archaeologist Charles Newton in the 19th century. Broken pieces of the 36 columns that once sat under the tomb’s pyramid are scattered all around, while steps lead down to Mausolus and Artemesia’s burial chamber. The mausoleum’s drainage system has also survived.
Newton transported the prize pieces to the British Museum in London, but some original friezes and recently discovered architectural fragments are on display in the park’s small museum.
However, surviving relics from the Halicarnassus era, and from the mausoleum itself, are still found throughout Bodrum and as far as 2,000 miles beyond.
Together, these archaeological puzzle pieces build a picture of life, and death, in one of antiquity’s most thriving harbor cities. Here’s how to follow the treasure trail.
Bodrum’s horseshoe-shaped Antique Theater , built during Mausolus’s reign and then expanded 200 years later during the Roman era, is a 20-minute walk uphill from the mausoleum site.
The theater looks out over the bay towards Bodrum Castle, the construction of which was fortified in the 15th century with marble columns and green volcanic stone from the ruins of the mausoleum.
At its peak, up to 10,000 people could be seated here to view everything from theatrical plays, to gladiator battles, to wild animal fights.
Entertainment today is more sedate. Concerts and cultural events are still held here, to audiences of nearly 4,000, but on the day CNN visits we share this space with just a well-behaved school group and one selfie-taking couple.
Mount Nemrut: Where colossal stone gods guard a 2,000-year-old mystery
Mausolus “built a lot of things back in those days,” says Can. “He made Caria more Greek. He started making people worship Greek gods and goddesses. He started to build temples for them.”
His expensive projects earned him a reputation as a tyrant, with finds raised through taxes, including one reputedly on Lycian men’s hair.
“He said to them, ‘give me your long hair, or you pay me tax,’” explains Can. “But he wasn’t wasting the hair. He was using them for the wigs of aristocrat Persians.”
One of these projects was building defensive walls around the city. Two gates guarded the east and the west of Halicarnassus, with the remains of the western Myndos Gate still standing on a hillside in the Eskiçeşme neighborhood, within walking distance of the theater.
The original height of the monumental towers of andesite stone is not known, but their sturdy bases have stood for close to 2,400 years. There is also a fourth-century necropolis nearby with Roman and Hellenistic vaulted tombs.
One of the most poignant parts of the site is the 23-feet-wide, eight-feet-deep moat which, during the Siege of Halicarnassus in 334 BCE, for some time held off the forces of Alexander the Great. Many soldiers lost their lives by falling into the moat or being trampled upon, while the collapse of an overloaded bridge also resulted in many casualties.
Back down on the waterfront, Bodrum Castle, an imposing example of Gothic architecture with Ottoman additions, dominates the modern town and also offers the city’s best views over the bay. It’s been on the UNESCO Tentative List of World Heritage sites since 2016.
It was built by the Knights of Saint John, who ruled over Bodrum throughout the 15th century. Not only were parts of Mausolus’s tomb used in the castle’s construction, but the castle is on the same promontory regarded to be the likely site of Mausolus’s palace .
For your 20-euro entrance fee, it’s a multiple-whammy historical experience. As well as being home to the Museum of Underwater Archaeology , it has a wealth of artifacts from the many civilizations that have called this corner of the world home. Its display related to the late Bronze Age Mycenaean people is particularly impressive.
The ancient monastery hanging from the side of a cliff
To see the remains of a woman who was likely the little sister of Mausoleus and Artemesia, head to the Carian Princess exhibit in the museum’s upper levels.
A stone sarcophagus was found in 1989 at a necropolis site in the Yokuşbaşı neighborhood of Bodrum containing a well-preserved skeleton of a high-born woman, along with a gold crown and jewels. She is believed to be Ada, fifth ruler of the Hecatomnid dynasty. Her remains are on display in the museum, along with her belongings and a full-size model based on a facial reconstruction of her skull.
Hecatomnus was Caria’s first indigenous satrap — the term for regional governors in the Persian empire — and ruled from 395 to 377 BCE. Of his five children, two sets of siblings married each other, with the brother-sister couple Idrieus and Ada succeeding Mausoleus and Artemesia.
Neither couple had children, so the marriages may have been symbolic. Sibling marriage was not at all common at this time, with incest generally considered taboo.
“I think back in those days, for royal people, it was okay to do anything they want to do,” says Can. The general population “were accepting whatever they did.”
Intermarriage between the siblings strengthened the dynasty by keeping the bloodline in the family. It also mirrored the mythology of the Greek gods, such as the union of king Zeus and his queen and sister-wife Hera.
Ada’s unusual high-status connections don’t end with the marriage to her brother Idrieus. She ruled over Caria twice, with reigns before and after the Siege of Halicarnassus, having being reinstated to power by her adopted son, Alexander the Great.
The shoreline around Bodrum is lined with beachside restaurants, beaches and bars, but it’s still possible to leave the crowds behind and ascend into the quiet forests of its mountainous interior. Here, the landscape is much as it was in ancient times.
Hidden high on a hilltop and visited by few, just a few miles’ hike from Bodrum town center, is the ancient city of Pedasa, which dates as far back as the 12th century BCE. In the fourth century, Mausolus ruled that the inhabitants of Pedasa and other smaller settlements be relocated to Halicarnassus, to boost the population of the newly established capital.
Pedasa is a stop on the 510-mile Carian Trail , a long-distance hiking route around the region that visits beaches, hills, villages and archaeological wonders. “In Turkey, there are so many ruins, and there’s so many civilizations, and we wanted to focus on the Carian features,” Altay Özcan, co-founder of the trail, tells CNN. Despite the area’s popularity with tourists, it’s still possible for visitors to get “a stretch of nature to yourself,” he says.
Pedasa is a “hidden gem,” says Can, as is Labraunda , “a sanctuary of Zeus. It’s on top of a mountain in the middle of nowhere and it’s like a little Machu Picchu. Idrieus, the brother of Mausolus, built most of it.”
Shortly before his death of unknown causes, Mausolus survived an assassination attempt during a royal procession at Labraunda during an annual festival. The ruins are about an hour’s drive from Bodrum, on the other side of Bodrum-Milas Airport.
What really happens inside a Turkish bath
It’s hard to go far in Turkey without tripping over an archaeological treasure, but there are still plenty more wonders hidden underground.
Gümüşlük is a pretty fishing village on the Bodrum Peninsula’s western coast, known for its seaside restaurants. At low tide, you can wade out from the harborside mermaid restaurant along the “King’s Road,” an ancient path that may date back 3,500 years to the Mycenaean era. It leads to a grassy mound known as Rabbit Island, the visible tip of what was once the city of Myndos, established by the Lelegian civilization some 4,000 years ago.
The island is fenced off due to uncompleted excavation work, but the city itself is thought to extend underground through Gümüşlük itself.
Two lion sculptures from the mausoleum now stand at the entrance of the British Museum’s Front Hall in London. The main mausoleum exhibit is in the museum’s Room 21, with other pieces in Rooms 77 and 81.
The walls are a gentle gray-blue, like the sea on a winter’s day, and the sand-colored tiles underfoot complement the marble statues and the slab friezes that line the room.
A colossal statue of a horse, from the chariot group which crowned the tomb, stands at the top of the staircase with head bowed and muscles flaring.
The friezes depict battles between Greeks and Amazons and Greek and Centaurs. In the Amazon frieze, a female warrior prepares to strike a kneeling Greek, while another Amazon appears to cry out for mercy as a caped Greek pulls her back by the hair.
In the center of the room are the two statues traditionally identified as Artemesia and Mausolus, both well over eight feet tall. Their poses are relaxed, their tunics and gathered mantles draped over their chest and thighs to their sandaled feet.
Artemesia’s face is shattered stone, but above it remains her hairstyle of three rolls of curls under a fitted cap. Mausolus’s head, with its wavy hair reaching shoulders some three feet wide, is largely intact. Under arched brows in a full, handsome face, his deep-set eyes gaze imperiously, thoughtfully, the hint of an Elvis pout curling at his lips.
Two-thousand miles from home, more than 2,000 years from their place in history, these effigies of brother and sister, of husband and wife, look blindly down on the stream of visitors in a future they could never have imagined.
The tomb which held them, the robust structure from which they hoped to stand forever over Bodrum and the blue Aegean, was lost centuries ago to the crashing waves of nature, which wash over all.

title: Secrets of the sultan’s palace where concubines and eunuchs lived | CNN
summary: Istanbul’s Topkapi Palace was the seat of power for the Ottoman Empire for nearly 400 years. A vast 700,000-square-meter walled labryinth, it was a bustling city within a city.
author: Maureen O'Hare
article:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This CNN Travel series may have adjacent ads by the country it highlights. CNN retains full editorial control over subject matter, reporting and frequency of the articles and videos, in compliance with our policy .
Some nations and empires declare their magnificence with monumental public displays: mighty castles and fortresses which ring across the skyline in loud exclamations of stone or brick.
Istanbul’s Topkapi Palace, seat of the Ottoman Empire for almost four centuries, is a little different.
Despite the opulence of the 15th-century Imperial Gate that marks its entrance, the palace is, in fact, a little hard to find.
This is in no small part due to the sheer number of UNESCO World Heritage sites spread across the wide public squares of Sultanahmet, Istanbul’s power nucleus since the Byzantine era.
Tourists line the cobblestone streets, dwarfed by the neighborhood’s grand scale as they make their way in and out of big-hitter landmarks such as the Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque and the Basilica Cistern.
However, all these resplendent sites occupy just a fraction of the footprint of Topkapi Palace’s sprawling 700,000-square-meter labyrinth, hidden on all sides by a five-kilometer walled perimeter up to 12 meters in height.
This was imperial power asserting itself through an architectural display of hierarchy and inaccessibility.
At its 17th-century peak, the Ottoman empire stretched across three continents, from Vienna to Algiers to Mecca.
T oday, Topkapi is considered one of the world’s greatest surviving palaces, alongside other regal estates such as France’s Palace of Versailles and China’s Forbidden City.
The palace was its “beating heart,” says Caroline Finkel, author of “Osman’s Dream: The History of the Ottoman Empire 1300-1923.” “All the intrigue” and “a lot of the action” took place within these walls.
Seraglio Point, a commanding promontory overlooking the waters where the Bosphorus Strait, the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara converge, is, by any measure, a prime piece of real estate.
Strategically positioned on a peninsula at the every edge of Europe, in the seventh century BCE, when the city was known as Byzantium, it was the site of the acropolis.
Those ancient walls were incorporated in the new defences when Sultan Mehmed II, who led the Siege on Constantinople which ended the Byzantine  Empire, ordered the palace’s construction in 1459.
Today, there are so many dozens of buildings, pavilions, kiosks and interconnected structures in the Topkapi Palace complex, and hundreds and hundreds of rooms, that it can be rightly termed as “countless”: There is no official number.
However, as Gülru Necipoglu notes in “Architecture, Ceremonial, and Power: The Topkapi Palace in the Fifteenth and Sixteenth Centuries,” the original layout and its main buildings remain remarkably intact.
By the 16th century and the empire’s Golden Age under Süleyman the Magnificent, the palace had reached its definitive configuration: “Thereafter, for hundreds of years its basic structure remained astonishingly intact, despite continuous restoration and rebuilding, almost as if it were forbidden to tamper with its essential form.”
The palace is made up of four courtyards and the 400-room harem where the Sultan and his family lived, and which no unrelated male could enter unless he was a eunuch.
Back when Topkapi was a bustling mini-city of some 4,000 people, each courtyard was increasingly restricted in access to the unauthorizsed.
She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World
The first is the largest and, in Ottoman times, was open to any unarmed member of the public.
Stepping in after the long entrance lines outside, it’s a blessed relief to step into the calming world of this beautiful tree-lined forecourt. The centuries-old plane and cypress trees are all the more remarkable because many of them are completely hollow, attacked by a fungus which destroyed the insides but left the trees still standing.
The Imperial Mint is here, the sixth-century Hagia Irene Church and the palace bakeries. Among the many picturesque fountains that adorn the space is one with a grisly legend attached: The Fountain of the Executioner is reputed to have been where the chief swordsman would have cleaned up after a beheading.
The Gate of Salutation, with its facade reminiscent of a European medieval castle, is where things get serious. This marked the transition into the Sultan’s private realm and only the reigning Sultan and the Queen Mother were allowed to enter on horseback; all lesser souls had to dismount and walk.
“At this point silence was imposed,” writes Necipoglu, drawing upon a depiction of an ambassadorial procession compiled for the Habsburg ambassador Johannes Lewenklau around 1586. “Those who broke it were beaten with a stick.”
The Second Courtyard is where the Grand Vizier, the Empire’s chief minister, led meetings in the Imperial Council building. The Sultan himself would observe proceedings from behind a gilded lattice screen, in an extra layer of seclusion.
The palace’s many structures might be modest in scale — few are over two stories — but the Ottoman designs and interior ornamentation are breathtaking in the Council building and elsewhere.
The former palace kitchens, now museum galleries, are also in this section, with one of the world’s largest collections of Chinese and Japanese porcelain.
The level of intricate detail in every gold-leafed arch or wall studded with thousands of delicately painted Iznik tiles could be studied for months, if not years.
At the Gate of Felicity, leading to the more intimately sized third courtyard, tourists pose with guards in the uniform of the Ottoman silahtar, in scenes reminiscent of visitors larking beside the motionless King’s Guard at England’s Buckingham Palace.
The palace museum, as it is today, is like an empty stage set, writes Necipoglu, but in the 15th and 16th century, “the palatial complex was a collection of workshops, armories, hospitals, stables, kitchens, bakeries, baths, audience halls, treasuries, libraries, archives, small mosques, dormitories, pavilions, sports grounds, zoological parks, pools, fountains, and gardens, housing thousands of inhabitants grouped according to the inner (private) and outer (public) services of the royal household.”
The third courtyard was divided into male and female sections. Slave pages resided in the dormitories and in the palace school they were educated, under the close watch of eunuchs, to occupy high positions as government bureaucrats. Male pages and female concubines alike were brought up in a common court culture, writes Necipoglu, and were eventually married off to one another. This created an in-house ruling elite which kept power centralized and out of the hands of the hereditary aristocracy beyond the palace walls.
Hagia Sophia: Secrets of the 1,600-year-old megastructure that has survived the collapse of empires
Visitors to the sultan could go to the Audience Chamber and no further, at which point they had to adhere to strict customs.
Süleyman the Magnificent “grew increasingly arrogant in his ceremonial practice, which eventually reached a peak of haughtiness by the last quarter of the sixteenth century,” writes Necipoglu. Ambassadors were flanked by guards like prisoners brought to the bar, and required to stand throughout. Instead of speaking to the sultan “they were only allowed to catch a momentary glimpse of the idollike sultan, who had grown almost too sacred to be seen.”
One of the must-visit spots in the third courtyard is the Treasury, filled with “relics of all sorts that had been given in gift exchanges,” says Finkel, as well as the 86-carat Spoonmakers’ Diamond and emerald-encrusted Topkapi Dagger.
The imperial harem, which runs alongside also in the third courtyard, has historically been the most misunderstood by Westerners, with their exoticized fever dreams of the Ottoman East.
This was where the Sultan lived with his children and the female members of his family.
As well as his wives, there were the concubines, enslaved women brought from across the empire.
In the 16th century, Hürrem Sultan broke tradition by rising from being a concubine slave to being the legal wife of Suleiman the Magnificent and one of the most powerful women in Ottoman history. The famous love letters between the two are testament to a strong and enduring passion.
Inside Turkey’s incredible underground city
However, for many women, these sequestered rooms —– with some of the most lavish ornamentation in all the palace —- were a gilded cage.
“In a way, it’s very sad,” says Finkel. It’s very impressive on one hand, but the conditions in which these poor women were living are not what one would want for oneself. In the rooms of the favorites, obviously, there were furnishings to make it a bit cozier,” but the dormitory-style accommodation for the rank and file is considerably more spartan.
The harem was guarded by Black eunuchs, African men who were enslaved and castrated as young boys. While castration was forbidden under Islamic law, the boys had been emasculated by their slave traders and so the practice continued right up until the end of the Ottoman Empire in 1923.
The palace hierarchies extended to race as well as gender. The Black eunuchs, with this close proximity to the royal household, were in an elevated position compared to the White eunuchs — typically enslaved Christians from the Balkans and Caucasus — who held sway as administrators, gatekeepers and supervisors of the pages.
The fourth courtyard, on the most elevated part of the promontory, was the sultan’s private retreat. Today, with its pretty pavilions and landscaped gardens, it’s easy to see the appeal.
“There’s a wonderful terrace where you can look out over the city and across the Bosphorus,” says Finkel. The skyline has changed “but you can imagine how it must have been,” standing at the edge of a continent, master of all you survey.

title: Hidden ‘ghost net’ crisis revealed in Mangrove Photography Awards | CNN
summary: The overall winner of the photography competition highlights the impact of abandoned fishing nets on mangroves.
author: Salome Grouard
article:
EDITOR’S NOTE: Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet Initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.
For years, Gaurav Patil has seen abandoned fishing nets snag and tangle in India’s mangroves. They’re known as “ghost nets” and can break down into microplastics, choke the coastal trees and disrupt the ecosystem.
Motivated to expose this “overlooked” crisis, he took his camera to a tide-swept shore of Nandgaon village, Maharashtra, south of Mumbai, and captured an image of a tree at night, using a 13-second UV exposure that gave an eerie glow to the net caught in its canopy. The resulting image is the overall winner of the 2026 Mangrove Photography Awards.
“I came across this particular patch where discarded fishing nets were getting trapped,” explained the marine-biologist-turned-photographer, in his photo submission. “It is not an uncommon sight, but it has been overlooked by most of us and the issue remains unresolved. (So) I wanted to document it in an artistic manner to grab the attention of the viewers.”
Titled “Tangled glow: When life meets the ruins,” the captivating photograph puts a spotlight on a crisis that has been quietly unfolding for years.
He brought over 600 water bodies back to life. His next mission: saving India’s vanishing stepwells
India is home to nearly 5,000 square kilometers (1,931 square miles) of mangrove cover spread across its coastline, including 40% of the largest mangrove forest in the world, The Sundarbans, with the remainder in neighboring Bangladesh. The trees are vital coastal barriers that shelter endangered species, prevent shoreline erosion, store up to four times more carbon per acre than tropical rainforests, and sustain millions of livelihoods through fisheries and tourism. But this precious ecosystem is facing mounting threats.
As well as “ghost nets,” rising sea levels, aquaculture — such as shrimp farms — and coastal development are taking their toll. In December 2025, the Bombay High Court approved a road-building project that could affect more than 45,000 mangrove trees along Mumbai’s western coast. Yet conservation of these forests could be part of the solution to urban flooding.
“Mangroves are increasingly at risk worldwide, but Gaurav Patil managed to capture an urgent threat that echoed all around the world, and has been going under the radar,” Leo Thom, creative director and founder of the Mangrove Photography Awards, told CNN. “Abandoned fishing gear is quiet and destructive, slowly choking the plant, releasing microplastics into the ecosystem, and persisting for decades.”
The problem extends far beyond India’s shores. The WWF estimated that 500,000 to 1 million tons of fishing equipment are abandoned in the ocean every year. An IUCN Red List of Ecosystems assessment found that more than half of global mangroves are at risk of collapse by 2050.
The diversity at stake is vast: other commended images in the awards show wildlife seeking refuge in mangroves across the world, from jungle cat kittens and royal Bengal tigers in India, to bottlenose dolphins in the US and Nile monitors in Gambia, West Africa.
“Storytelling is such a big part of the protection of these ecosystems, and we’re also hoping that the awards will contribute to raising awareness on how to restore their habitats properly,” Thom added. “Money is just being poured on mass planting projects that aren’t successful,” he continued, adding that research has found hydrology — re-establishing the natural flow of water into degraded mangrove ecosystems — to be beneficial, “as it’ll allow the mangrove to spread naturally without human intervention.”
Protecting Sri Lanka’s precious mangroves
One of the award categories is dedicated to conservation and restoration. The winning image, taken by Garry Lotulung, shows Pasijah, a 56-year-old resident of Bedono in Central Java, Indonesia, planting mangrove seedlings after yet another flood submerged her village. In 2021, she and her son planted 15,000 seedlings in a single day; by the next morning, the waves had washed them all away.
“It’s precisely this kind of story that will help us spread awareness,” Thom said. “When we started, we had less than 100 submissions. This year, which marks our 12th edition, we received more than 5,000 of them — and it shows that more and more people are realizing how crucial mangroves are for climate resilience and coastal protection.”

title: Nature’s cleanup crew: Stunning photos show vultures in a different light | CNN
summary: Conservationists hope the competition can help improve the public’s perception of vultures.
author: Amy Gunia
article:
EDITOR’S NOTE: Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet Initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.
It can be hard to get people to care about protecting vultures. They aren’t exactly cute and cuddly, and their diet of dead animals doesn’t help.
Conservationists hope a vulture photography competition can help improve the public’s perception of the animals, which play an important ecological role by disposing of carrion.
“People tend to think they’re ugly,” says André Botha, Africa Projects Manager at the Hawk Conservancy Trust, one of the groups behind International Vulture Awareness Day, which organizes the contest. “If you don’t like it, you won’t conserve it.”
One of the world’s largest flying birds is making a comeback
The Vulture Interactions photography contest, running for its second year, announced its results on July 20. The winning photos show various vulture species in action, from the bearded vulture, Europe’s rarest vulture, to the California condor, of which there are only about 600 birds left in existence.
Globally, there are 23 vulture species, living on every continent except Australia and Antarctica. Many face serious threats to their survival.
Species in Asia and Africa are “under tremendous pressure,” says Botha. Of the 16 Old World species, which live across Africa, Asia and Europe, seven are critically endangered, and two more are endangered, he says.
He hopes the contest can “make people aware not to judge the vulture book by its cover, but to understand the animal better and (be aware) how incredibly important it is.”
When vultures eat dead animals, it helps to stop the spread of disease from rotting meat and saves humans the work of cleaning it up. “There is no other animal on the planet that is designed to do what vultures do,” says Botha, who is also the co-chair of the vulture specialist group at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
Energy infrastructure — from power lines to wind turbines — and habitat fragmentation threaten vulture populations. Vultures can also be the target of poachers, who sell their body parts. The birds have excellent eyesight, with the ability to spot a three-foot-long carcass from four miles away . Some people buy their heads, believing that will give them the power of foresight.
Poisoning is the main threat. Poachers sometimes intentionally poison vultures, to stop them from circling overhead and drawing attention to their catch. Sometimes people poison predators like lions or hyenas, which in turn kills vultures when they eat the carcasses.
Bringing back Andean condors from the brink of extinction
In India, diclofenac, an anti-inflammatory drug, was introduced for veterinary use in the 1990s. The drug, which causes kidney failure in vultures that eat animals treated with it, resulted in the death of 95% of the country’s wild vultures in the second half of the decade.
One study found that may have resulted in 500,000 excess human deaths over five years in the early 2000s, without vultures to stop the spread of disease, and to crowd out feral dogs and rats, which can both pass on infections to humans.
Botha says that he hopes the photography contest can help boost understanding of the crucial role vultures play — even if people still don’t find them aesthetically pleasing. “People will judge them because of what they look like,” he says. “It might be a grudging appreciation for what they do.”
He also hopes the contest can help get more people interested in vulture conservation: “We need to have a younger generation of people to step in and carry the flag forward.”
